text: Claude Bourdet (28 October 1909 – 20 March 1996) was a writer, journalist, polemist, and militant French politician. He was the son of the dramatic author Édouard Bourdet and the poet Catherine Pozzi, and was born and died in Paris, France. In 1935, he married Ida Adamoff. He left the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich with an engineering diploma in technical physics in 1933. After completing his military service in the Artillerie de Montagne, he was assigned to a mission for the Economy Ministry during the government of the Front populaire. Bourdet was active in French Resistance movements and participated in the foundation of the resistance newspaper Combat alongside Henri Frenay. He served on the management committee of Combat until Frenay's departure to London and later Algeria in 1943, when Bourdet became its representative. From 1942, he contributed to the creation and development of the newspaper, focusing on dividing public administrations. In 1944, he was arrested by the Gestapo, imprisoned at Fresnes, and subsequently deported to various concentration camps, including Neuengamme, Sachsenhausen, and Buchenwald. After the war, he continued writing for Combat, but due to a conflict with Henri Smadja, the newspaper's owner, he left in 1950. In 1950, with the assistance of Gilles Martinet and Roger Stéphane, he founded L’Observateur, which was renamed L’Observateur Aujourd’hui in 1953 and then France-Observateur in 1954. Bourdet advocated for the union of the left and social justice and supported the anti-colonial struggle, condemning repression in Madagascar and torture in Algeria. In 1961, he investigated and denounced Maurice Papon, the prefect of the police, in relation to the shootings of Algerian FLN demonstrators on 17 October of that year, known as the Paris massacre of 1961. His political activism led to a major rift within the France-Observateur team in 1963, resulting in his departure from the publication. He continued to publish articles in Témoignage chrétien, Politique Hebdo, or Politis, and participated in special issues of the Nouvel Observateur. In 1985, Bourdet was a member of the "Jury of Honor" that evaluated whether the film Des terroristes à la retraite should be aired in France. The "Jury of Honor" reported that while it was desirable for a film to inform French audiences of all generations about the FTP-MOI saga, such a film had not yet been made. Bourdet described the film as "racist and anti-Semitic."
